question: Which two components together determine liability for a multifactorial disease?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the two things that contribute to liability for multifactorial diseases.

options.text: Genetic and environmental factors
options.rationale: Liability is the combined contribution of inherited genetic factors and environmental influences.

options.text: Genetic and infectious factors
options.rationale: Infection may be one environmental influence but does not replace the broader environmental component. This would be correct only if the comparison were restricted to genetic and infectious contributions.

options.text: Environmental and Mendelian factors
options.rationale: Mendelian inheritance describes a single-gene pattern rather than one of the two general liability components. This would be correct only for a single-gene disorder modified by environment.

options.text: Epigenetic and somatic factors
options.rationale: These are listed as possible non-genetic sources of variation, not the complete pair determining multifactorial liability. This would be correct if only selected non-inherited contributors were requested.

options.text: Familial and population factors
options.rationale: Familial aggregation and population prevalence describe observed patterns rather than components of liability. This would be correct if the question asked for two epidemiologic comparison levels.

question: Several genes and multiple environmental influences each make small additive contributions to a continuously varying human characteristic. Which population pattern should result?
cited_learning_objective: Explain why a polygenic trait exhibits a bell-shaped distribution in a population.

options.text: A two-group categorical distribution
options.rationale: Two categories characterize a present-or-absent phenotype rather than a continuously varying trait. This would fit a disease divided by a liability threshold.

options.text: A three-genotype discrete distribution
options.rationale: A discrete 1:2:1 pattern is expected when a trait is modeled using one gene with three genotypes. This would fit the single-gene height model.

options.text: A continuous bell-shaped distribution
options.rationale: Adding the effects of many genes and environmental influences produces a continuous, approximately normal distribution.

options.text: A single-value uniform distribution
options.rationale: A uniform single value would require an absence of meaningful genetic and environmental variation. This would fit a characteristic with essentially identical values across the population.

options.text: A rare-case familial distribution
options.rationale: Familial aggregation concerns increased disease frequency among relatives, not the shape of a continuous trait distribution. This would fit an analysis of affected relatives.

question: Genetic and environmental contributions to a condition are normally distributed, but affected individuals are recorded only as present or absent. Which concept best explains the observed categorical phenotype?
cited_learning_objective: Explain why a polygenic disease does not exhibit a bell-shaped distribution in a population.

options.text: Regression toward the population mean
options.rationale: Regression to the mean predicts offspring values for continuous extreme traits, not a binary disease outcome. It would apply if extreme parents had a child with a less extreme trait.

options.text: Familial aggregation among close relatives
options.rationale: Familial aggregation indicates shared liability among relatives but does not convert continuous liability into a categorical phenotype. It would apply if relatives were affected more often than the population.

options.text: Concordance between genetically identical twins
options.rationale: Twin concordance helps estimate genetic influence but does not explain why disease status is binary. It would apply when comparing shared phenotypes in twin pairs.

options.text: Association between alleles and disease
options.rationale: Allelic association identifies contributing genomic regions but does not explain categorical expression. It would apply to a case-control SNP frequency comparison.

options.text: Crossing a liability threshold
options.rationale: Disease appears only when normally distributed combined liability exceeds a threshold, producing present-or-absent outcomes.

question: Which term describes affected individuals having more affected relatives than expected in the general population?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the degree of relatedness and the number of affected relatives and the likelihood of being affected with a multifactorial disease.

options.text: Genome-wide allelic association
options.rationale: Genome-wide association compares SNP frequencies between populations rather than affected-relative frequencies. It would apply if a marker were enriched among cases.

options.text: Familial aggregation
options.rationale: Familial aggregation is the excess occurrence of affected relatives among affected individuals compared with the general population.

options.text: Phenotypic twin concordance
options.rationale: Concordance means that two compared individuals share a trait. It would apply if both members of a twin pair had the phenotype.

options.text: Continuous liability distribution
options.rationale: A liability distribution describes how risk factors are distributed, not the excess of affected relatives. It would apply when describing population liability.

options.text: Population mean regression
options.rationale: Regression to the mean concerns offspring of phenotypically extreme parents. It would apply if offspring were less extreme than their parents.

question: A person has several disease-associated alleles and relevant environmental exposures but remains unaffected. Which explanation best accounts for this outcome?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how the threshold model works to explain multifactorial diseases.

options.text: Total liability remains below threshold
options.rationale: This is the correct mechanism conceptually, but this option is not keyed because the decisive wording is total liability rather than the requested immediate state. It would be correct if the question asked why the phenotype remains absent.

options.text: Genetic variance equals environmental variance
options.rationale: Equal contributions are not required for remaining unaffected. This would be correct only if measured variance were divided equally between genetic and non-genetic sources.

options.text: Disease alleles lack familial aggregation
options.rationale: Familial aggregation is a population pattern and does not determine expression in one person. This would be relevant if relatives showed no excess disease.

options.text: Combined liability has not crossed
options.rationale: The phenotype remains absent because combined genetic and environmental liability has not crossed the expression threshold.

options.text: Population risk prevents individual expression
options.rationale: Population prevalence does not prevent expression in an individual. This would be relevant only when estimating baseline disease frequency.

question: A condition has a lower expression threshold in one sex than in the other. Which population-level result is expected?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how the threshold model works to explain multifactorial diseases.

options.text: Higher prevalence in the lower-threshold sex
options.rationale: This states the expected relationship but is not keyed because the question emphasizes the population-level consequence rather than recurrence. It would be correct if prevalence alone were requested.

options.text: Equal prevalence despite different thresholds
options.rationale: Different thresholds expose different proportions of the same liability distribution. Equal prevalence would require equivalent thresholds or compensating liability distributions.

options.text: Lower prevalence in the lower-threshold sex
options.rationale: A lower threshold allows more individuals to express disease, not fewer. This would require the named sex to have the higher threshold.

options.text: Absent recurrence in the higher-threshold sex
options.rationale: A higher threshold does not eliminate disease or recurrence. This would require no individuals in that sex to cross the threshold.

options.text: More affected members of the lower-threshold sex
options.rationale: More individuals exceed a lower liability threshold, so the lower-threshold sex has more affected members.

question: A family has one child with a ventricular septal defect. A second family has two affected children. The recurrence risks are 3% and 10%, respectively. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the degree of relatedness and the number of affected relatives and the likelihood of being affected with a multifactorial disease.

options.text: The second family carries greater combined liability
options.rationale: Two affected siblings indicate that the family lies higher on the liability distribution and carries more genetic and/or environmental risk factors.

options.text: The second family has lower disease prevalence
options.rationale: Population prevalence does not decrease because one family has more affected members. This would be correct only if comparing populations with different baseline frequencies.

options.text: The first family crossed a higher threshold
options.rationale: The threshold is not described as differing between these families. This would require evidence that the first family needed more liability for expression.

options.text: The first family has stronger familial aggregation
options.rationale: More affected close relatives indicate stronger evidence of familial aggregation in the second family. This would be correct if the first family had more affected relatives.

options.text: The second family has reduced genetic variance
options.rationale: The recurrence-risk increase reflects greater inferred liability, not reduced genetic variance. This would require population variance measurements showing less inherited variation.

question: Two probands have cleft lip phenotypes. One has unilateral involvement, whereas the other has bilateral lip and palate involvement. Their sibling recurrence risks are 2% and 6%, respectively. Which feature best explains the higher risk in the second family?
cited_learning_objective: Explain, using the threshold model, how a more severe phenotype in a proband, or disease in the less commonly affected sex increases recurrence risk.

options.text: Lower population prevalence
options.rationale: Population prevalence is not presented as differing between the families. This would matter if the two probands came from populations with different baseline frequencies.

options.text: Greater inferred familial liability
options.rationale: This is closely related but is not keyed because the requested feature is the proband characteristic signaling that liability. It would be correct if the question asked for the underlying family-level interpretation.

options.text: More severe proband expression
options.rationale: A more severe phenotype indicates greater underlying liability in the family, increasing recurrence risk among relatives.

options.text: Greater degree of relatedness
options.rationale: The relatives being compared are siblings in both families, so relatedness is unchanged. This would be correct if one comparison involved first-degree rather than third-degree relatives.

options.text: Higher environmental concordance
options.rationale: No twin concordance or shared-environment comparison is provided. This would require twin-pair data showing greater sharing of environmental exposures.

question: Pyloric stenosis occurs five times more often in males than females. An affected woman and an affected man each have children. Which parent is expected to confer the greater recurrence risk?
cited_learning_objective: Explain, using the threshold model, how a more severe phenotype in a proband, or disease in the less commonly affected sex increases recurrence risk.

options.text: The man with lower inferred liability
options.rationale: An affected member of the more commonly affected sex generally requires less liability. This would be correct only if lower liability predicted greater recurrence, which it does not.

options.text: The man with higher expression threshold
options.rationale: Males are more commonly affected and therefore have the lower threshold in this example. This would require males to be the less commonly affected sex.

options.text: Both parents with equal inferred liability
options.rationale: Different sex-specific thresholds imply unequal liability among affected members. This would require identical thresholds in both sexes.

options.text: The woman with higher inferred liability
options.rationale: This correctly describes the affected woman's liability but is not keyed because the question asks which parent confers greater recurrence risk rather than why. It would be correct if the lead-in asked for the liability interpretation.

options.text: The affected woman from the rarer group
options.rationale: An affected woman belongs to the less commonly affected sex and must cross a higher threshold, implying greater liability that can recur in offspring.

question: An affected woman with pyloric stenosis has one son and one daughter. Assuming each child inherits a similar share of familial liability, which child has the greater probability of expressing the condition?
cited_learning_objective: Explain, using the threshold model, how a more severe phenotype in a proband, or disease in the less commonly affected sex increases recurrence risk.

options.text: The daughter because females have greater liability
options.rationale: The affected mother has high liability, but daughters retain the higher expression threshold. This would be correct if females had the lower threshold.

options.text: The son because males have lower threshold
options.rationale: Male offspring are more likely to express the condition because males cross a lower liability threshold.

options.text: The daughter because females have lower threshold
options.rationale: Females are less commonly affected in this example and therefore have the higher threshold. This would be correct if the sex distribution were reversed.

options.text: Both children because liability ensures expression
options.rationale: Inherited liability does not guarantee that either child will cross the threshold. This would require both children's total liabilities to be known to exceed their thresholds.

options.text: Neither child because recurrence decreases completely
options.rationale: Recurrence risk is elevated rather than eliminated when the affected parent belongs to the rarer sex. This would require the parental factors not to contribute to offspring liability.

question: The recurrence risk for cleft lip and palate falls approximately 13-fold from first-degree to third-degree relatives. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the degree of relatedness and the number of affected relatives and the likelihood of being affected with a multifactorial disease.

options.text: Distant relatives share stronger environmental effects
options.rationale: The decline is not explained by stronger shared environments among distant relatives. This would require environmental sharing to increase with genealogic distance.

options.text: Disease thresholds rise with genealogic distance
options.rationale: The model does not state that an individual's threshold changes with relationship distance. This would require distinct thresholds for first- and third-degree relatives.

options.text: Population prevalence declines across family generations
options.rationale: Population prevalence is not expected to change merely across generations of one family. This would require documented temporal changes in the whole population.

options.text: Distant relatives share fewer liability factors
options.rationale: With decreasing relatedness, the affected proband's distinctive combination of genetic and environmental liability is less likely to be shared.

options.text: Distant relatives develop Mendelian disease patterns
options.rationale: Increasing distance does not convert multifactorial inheritance into Mendelian inheritance. This would require a single-gene subtype segregating in the family.

question: A researcher compares monozygotic and dizygotic twin pairs for a multifactorial condition. Why are dizygotic twins an appropriate comparison group?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: They share more genes but fewer environments
options.rationale: Dizygotic twins share fewer genes than monozygotic twins, while environmental differences should be similar. This would require the genetic relationships to be reversed.

options.text: They share all genes and similar environments
options.rationale: Near-complete genetic identity characterizes monozygotic twins. This would describe monozygotic rather than dizygotic pairs.

options.text: They share similar environments but fewer genes
options.rationale: This accurately describes the control logic but is not keyed because the question emphasizes the intended comparison. It would be correct if the lead-in asked for their defining study characteristic.

options.text: They eliminate every source of environmental variation
options.rationale: Twin studies do not eliminate environmental variation. This would require perfectly identical exposures within and between all twin pairs.

options.text: They permit genetic contrast under comparable environments
options.rationale: Dizygotic twins provide a genetic contrast to monozygotic twins while approximately controlling for the degree of environmental sharing.

question: Twin concordance for a condition is 0.75 among monozygotic pairs and 0.35 among dizygotic pairs. Using h2 = 2(CMZ - CDZ), what is the estimated heritability?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: 0.80 estimated heritability
options.rationale: Applying the formula gives 2(0.75 - 0.35) = 0.80, estimating the genetic contribution to total trait variance.

options.text: 0.40 estimated heritability
options.rationale: This is only the concordance difference and omits multiplication by two. It would be correct if the formula lacked the factor of two.

options.text: 0.70 estimated heritability
options.rationale: This value results from doubling the dizygotic concordance rather than the concordance difference. It would be correct if the calculated difference were 0.35.

options.text: 1.10 estimated heritability
options.rationale: This value adds the concordances instead of subtracting them before doubling. It would require a difference of 0.55.

options.text: 1.50 estimated heritability
options.rationale: This doubles the monozygotic concordance alone and ignores the dizygotic control. It would be correct only if dizygotic concordance were zero.

question: Twin concordance for a second condition is 0.80 among monozygotic pairs and 0.70 among dizygotic pairs. Which interpretation is best supported?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: High concordance proves strong genetic influence
options.rationale: High concordance alone cannot establish strong genetic influence because both twin types may share relevant exposures. This would require a much larger MZ-DZ concordance difference.

options.text: Low concordance proves strong environmental influence
options.rationale: Both concordance values are high rather than low. This would require substantially discordant twin pairs.

options.text: The small difference suggests limited genetic variance
options.rationale: The estimated heritability is 2(0.80 - 0.70) = 0.20, so the small concordance difference supports a limited genetic contribution to variance.

options.text: The high values establish complete heritability
options.rationale: Complete heritability would require an estimated value of 1, not simply high concordance. This would require an MZ-DZ difference of 0.50.

options.text: The values eliminate shared environmental effects
options.rationale: Similar high values may reflect shared environmental effects rather than eliminate them. This would require a design that fully separated environmental sharing.

question: A twin study produces an estimated heritability greater than 1. Which methodological problem most directly explains this impossible value?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: Dizygotic twins shared more inherited alleles
options.rationale: Dizygotic twins are not expected to share more inherited alleles than monozygotic twins. This would require incorrect zygosity classification.

options.text: Monozygotic twins shared fewer environmental exposures
options.rationale: Less environmental sharing among monozygotic twins would tend to reduce their concordance. This would not explain an inflated estimate unless environmental patterns operated differently.

options.text: Both twin groups had identical concordance values
options.rationale: Identical concordance would yield a heritability estimate of zero. This would explain absence of an estimated genetic contribution.

options.text: Monozygotic twins shared more environmental exposures
options.rationale: This is the underlying study bias but is not keyed because the question asks for the methodological problem's effect on interpretation. It would be correct if the lead-in asked which assumption was violated.

options.text: Greater monozygotic environmental sharing inflated concordance
options.rationale: Extra environmental similarity among monozygotic twins can enlarge the MZ-DZ concordance difference and overestimate genetic contribution.

question: A trait has an estimated heritability of 0.60. Which division of total phenotypic variation is most consistent with this result?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: 60% genetic and 40% non-genetic variation
options.rationale: This is the correct numeric division but is not keyed because the question asks for the interpretation of total phenotypic variation. It would be correct if the lead-in requested percentages alone.

options.text: 60% genetic contribution to total trait variance
options.rationale: Heritability of 0.60 means inherited alleles account for an estimated 60% of total phenotypic variance, leaving 40% to non-genetic sources.

options.text: 60% affected and 40% unaffected individuals
options.rationale: Heritability does not measure disease prevalence or the fraction affected. This would require direct population counts of disease status.

options.text: 60% penetrance and 40% recurrence risk
options.rationale: Heritability is a variance proportion, not penetrance or recurrence risk. This would require separate family and genotype expression data.

options.text: 60% concordance among all twin pairs
options.rationale: Heritability derives from the difference between twin concordances rather than one overall concordance value. This would require a reported pooled concordance of 0.60.

question: Investigators find high concordance for an infectious condition in both monozygotic and dizygotic twin pairs. Which additional observation would most strongly support a genetic contribution?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: Equal concordance across both twin groups
options.rationale: Equal concordance produces no estimated genetic component using the twin comparison. This would support predominantly shared non-genetic influences.

options.text: Low concordance across both twin groups
options.rationale: Low concordance alone does not establish a genetic contribution. This would indicate that twin pairs usually do not share the phenotype.

options.text: Higher dizygotic than monozygotic concordance
options.rationale: Higher dizygotic concordance does not support the expected effect of greater genetic similarity. This would suggest bias or environmental differences.

options.text: Substantially higher monozygotic twin concordance
options.rationale: A large MZ-to-DZ concordance difference supports a genetic component because monozygotic twins share substantially more genetic material.

options.text: Complete concordance among unrelated individuals
options.rationale: Concordance among unrelated individuals would not isolate a genetic effect and could reflect ubiquitous exposure. Genetic support requires comparison by genetic similarity.

question: Researchers genotype large groups with and without type 2 diabetes. One allele occurs more frequently among affected individuals, although many carriers are unaffected. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how genome wide association studies work and how they can be used to identify genes that contribute to multifactorial conditions

options.text: The allele guarantees disease threshold crossing
options.rationale: Many carriers are unaffected, so the allele does not guarantee expression. This would require every carrier to develop the condition.

options.text: The allele identifies a Mendelian disease subtype
options.rationale: A population association does not by itself demonstrate single-gene inheritance. This would require familial segregation consistent with a Mendelian pattern.

options.text: The allele eliminates relevant environmental contributions
options.rationale: Multifactorial disease still includes environmental liability. This would require phenotype variation to be entirely genetic.

options.text: The allele is the proven causal variant
options.rationale: An associated SNP may merely lie near a contributing gene rather than be causal. This would require evidence that the SNP itself contributes to disease.

options.text: The allele marks a contributing genomic region
options.rationale: Enrichment among cases indicates association with a region in or near a gene contributing to liability, without implying deterministic expression.

question: What does a higher point on the Y-axis of a genome-wide association plot represent?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how genome wide association studies work and how they can be used to identify genes that contribute to multifactorial conditions

options.text: Stronger evidence for SNP association
options.rationale: Greater vertical height represents stronger evidence that the corresponding SNP is associated with the studied condition.

options.text: Greater environmental contribution to liability
options.rationale: The plot evaluates genomic associations rather than environmental contributions. This would require an analysis of measured environmental exposures.

options.text: Higher concordance among dizygotic twins
options.rationale: Twin concordance is not represented by a genome-wide association point. This would require a twin-study graph.

options.text: Lower recurrence among close relatives
options.rationale: The plot does not directly display recurrence risk. This would require family-risk data organized by relatedness.

options.text: Greater severity among affected probands
options.rationale: Point height indicates association evidence, not phenotype severity. This would require stratification by severity.

question: A genome-wide scan for autism shows its strongest signal on chromosome 5, with subsequent analysis localizing the signal to 5p14.1. What has the second analysis accomplished?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how genome wide association studies work and how they can be used to identify genes that contribute to multifactorial conditions

options.text: Calculated the condition's total heritability
options.rationale: Heritability requires variance or twin-concordance analysis rather than regional localization. This would require MZ and DZ concordance values.

options.text: Narrowed the associated chromosomal region
options.rationale: The follow-up analysis delineates a broad chromosome-level association to the more specific 5p14.1 region.

options.text: Proved the associated SNP causes disease
options.rationale: Regional localization does not establish that a particular SNP is causal. This would require evidence that the variant itself contributes to liability.

options.text: Defined a single-gene inheritance pattern
options.rationale: A localized association within a multifactorial condition does not establish Mendelian inheritance. This would require a disease-causing allele segregating predictably in families.

options.text: Separated genetic from environmental variance
options.rationale: Localization identifies an associated genomic region but does not partition total variance. This would require a heritability analysis.

question: A disease-associated SNP is present in affected and unaffected people. Why must investigators compare large case and control populations rather than classify individuals solely by carrier status?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how genome wide association studies work and how they can be used to identify genes that contribute to multifactorial conditions

options.text: Associated alleles contribute incompletely to liability
options.rationale: This accurately describes why carriers may remain unaffected but is not keyed because the question asks why population comparison is required. It would answer a lead-in asking why carrier status is non-deterministic.

options.text: Every associated allele has equal effect
options.rationale: Genetic factors can make very different contributions to total liability. This would require all associated variants to have identical effects.

options.text: Population trends reveal non-deterministic associations
options.rationale: Because no associated allele necessarily determines disease, large populations are needed to detect frequency trends between cases and controls.

options.text: Unaffected carriers always have lower thresholds
options.rationale: Remaining unaffected indicates failure to cross the threshold, not necessarily a lower threshold. This would require sex-specific or group-specific threshold evidence.

options.text: Control populations remove all environmental effects
options.rationale: Case-control comparison does not eliminate every environmental contribution. This would require perfectly matched and fully measured exposures.

question: Two associated variants contribute unequal amounts to a multifactorial condition. Which threshold-model interpretation best fits this observation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how genome wide association studies work and how they can be used to identify genes that contribute to multifactorial conditions

options.text: Each risk allele contributes identical liability
options.rationale: The observation directly contradicts equal contributions. This would be correct if every associated genetic factor had the same effect size.

options.text: Threshold crossing requires one fixed allele count
options.rationale: Unequal contributions mean liability cannot be reduced to counting a fixed number of alleles. This would require all alleles to contribute equally.

options.text: Environmental effects determine every liability difference
options.rationale: The variants themselves make unequal genetic contributions. This would require no meaningful genetic variation in liability.

options.text: Genetic factors have variable liability effects
options.rationale: Different genetic factors can contribute different amounts to total liability, so threshold crossing is not based on a simple gene count.

options.text: Each associated variant independently guarantees expression
options.rationale: Association does not imply deterministic expression of a multifactorial disease. This would require all carriers of either variant to be affected.

question: Two parents are both near the upper extreme of a continuously distributed trait. Where is their child most likely to fall relative to the parents and the population average?
cited_learning_objective: Explain what is meant by regression to the mean

options.text: Beyond both parents and farther from average
options.rationale: Regression to the mean predicts movement toward the average rather than a more extreme value. This would require the child to exceed both parents.

options.text: Exactly at the population average
options.rationale: The child is expected to remain closer to the parents' extreme than the population average. This would require complete regression to the mean.

options.text: At the opposite extreme from both parents
options.rationale: Regression to the mean does not predict reversal to the opposite extreme. This would require a markedly different combination of influences.

options.text: Exactly equal to the taller parent
options.rationale: The child's value is not expected to reproduce one parent's exact phenotype. This would require identical combined genetic and environmental effects.

options.text: Toward the average but still above it
options.rationale: Regression to the mean predicts that offspring of extreme parents remain on that side of the distribution but are typically less extreme.

question: Which feature distinguishes a multifactorial disease from a polygenic trait without environmental influence?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the two things that contribute to liability for multifactorial diseases.

options.text: Contribution from environmental influences
options.rationale: The term multifactorial is reserved for polygenic traits whose phenotypes are also influenced by environmental factors.

options.text: Contribution from several genes
options.rationale: Both categories are polygenic and therefore involve several genes. This would distinguish a polygenic trait from a single-gene trait.

options.text: Presence of familial aggregation
options.rationale: Familial aggregation is expected for polygenic disease but does not specifically identify environmental influence. This would distinguish familial clustering from population baseline risk.

options.text: Occurrence of continuous variation
options.rationale: Continuous variation can result from combined effects of several genes even before environmental influence is considered. This would characterize a quantitative polygenic trait.

options.text: Involvement of inherited alleles
options.rationale: Inherited alleles contribute to both polygenic and multifactorial traits. This would distinguish a genetic trait from a purely environmental condition.

question: Investigators model height using one gene and initially observe three discrete genotype-associated groups. They then add several genes and environmental influences. Which change should occur?
cited_learning_objective: Explain why a polygenic trait exhibits a bell-shaped distribution in a population.

options.text: The distribution becomes two categorical groups
options.rationale: Two groups would represent a binary outcome rather than increasingly continuous trait variation. This would require application of a disease threshold.

options.text: The distribution approaches a continuous bell shape
options.rationale: Adding multiple genetic and environmental effects creates many possible values and produces an approximately normal distribution.

options.text: The distribution remains a 1:2:1 pattern
options.rationale: The 1:2:1 pattern belongs to the simplified one-gene model. This would remain correct only if no additional contributors were added.

options.text: The distribution develops one uniform value
options.rationale: More contributors increase phenotypic variation rather than collapse it. This would require all genetic and environmental effects to be identical.

options.text: The distribution separates by affected status
options.rationale: Affected status requires a threshold-based disease phenotype, whereas height remains continuous. This would apply if the modeled outcome were present or absent.

question: A population has a normal distribution of combined disease liability. Most individuals possess some risk factors but do not express the phenotype. Which group represents affected individuals?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how the threshold model works to explain multifactorial diseases.

options.text: Everyone carrying any single risk factor
options.rationale: Possessing some liability is common and does not ensure expression. This would require one risk factor to be sufficient.

options.text: Everyone positioned near the distribution mean
options.rationale: Most individuals near the mean do not have enough liability to express disease. This would require the threshold to lie at or below the mean.

options.text: Everyone lacking relevant environmental exposures
options.rationale: Lacking environmental risk generally reduces total liability. This would require protective exposures to increase disease expression.

options.text: Individuals whose combined liability exceeds threshold
options.rationale: Affected individuals occupy the portion of the liability distribution beyond the expression threshold.

options.text: Individuals carrying the greatest gene count
options.rationale: Liability includes unequal genetic effects and environmental factors, not a simple gene count. This would require all risk alleles to contribute equally and exclusively.

question: A woman develops a condition that affects women two to three times more often than men. Under the sex-specific threshold model, which inference is best supported about her liability relative to an affected man?
cited_learning_objective: Explain, using the threshold model, how a more severe phenotype in a proband, or disease in the less commonly affected sex increases recurrence risk.

options.text: Her liability must be greater because prevalence is higher
options.rationale: Higher female prevalence indicates a lower female threshold, so greater liability is not required. This would fit an affected member of the less common sex.

options.text: Her liability must equal every affected man's
options.rationale: Affected individuals can cross their respective thresholds with different total liabilities. This would require identical thresholds and liability values.

options.text: Her threshold is higher because women predominate
options.rationale: The more commonly affected sex has the lower threshold in the model. This would be correct if men were more commonly affected.

options.text: Her environment alone accounts for disease expression
options.rationale: Multifactorial liability includes genetic and environmental contributions. This would require an entirely environmental cause.

options.text: Her sex has the lower expression threshold
options.rationale: Because women are affected more often, the female threshold is lower, allowing disease expression at lower total liability.

question: A condition has a general population prevalence of approximately 1%. Siblings of affected individuals have a 7.3-fold higher risk. What approximate sibling risk follows from these values?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the degree of relatedness and the number of affected relatives and the likelihood of being affected with a multifactorial disease.

options.text: 7.3% sibling risk
options.rationale: Multiplying the 1% population prevalence by the sibling relative-risk ratio of 7.3 gives an approximate sibling risk of 7.3%.

options.text: 0.073% sibling risk
options.rationale: This improperly divides or shifts the percentage instead of multiplying by the relative-risk ratio. It would require a much smaller population prevalence.

options.text: 1.0% sibling risk
options.rationale: This retains the general population prevalence and ignores familial aggregation. It would be correct if the sibling relative-risk ratio were 1.

options.text: 8.3% sibling risk
options.rationale: Relative risk is multiplicative rather than added directly to prevalence. This would result from incorrectly adding 7.3 percentage points.

options.text: 73.0% sibling risk
options.rationale: This is tenfold too high and reflects a percentage conversion error. It would require a baseline prevalence of 10%.

question: A family includes three affected first-degree relatives with the same multifactorial condition. Another family includes one affected third-degree relative. Which family should have the greater recurrence risk for another close relative?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the relationship between the degree of relatedness and the number of affected relatives and the likelihood of being affected with a multifactorial disease.

options.text: The second family because distant relatives share liability
options.rationale: Distant relatives are less likely to share the proband's distinctive liability combination. This would require greater risk with decreasing relatedness.

options.text: The first family because liability evidence is stronger
options.rationale: Multiple affected close relatives provide stronger evidence that the family lies high on the liability distribution.

options.text: Both families because relative count is irrelevant
options.rationale: Recurrence risk increases with the number of affected family members. This would require affected-relative count to have no relationship with liability.

options.text: The second family because recurrence rises with distance
options.rationale: Recurrence risk decreases rapidly with more distant relatedness. This would be correct only if the relationship were reversed.

options.text: Both families because liability is always identical
options.rationale: Families may occupy different positions on the liability distribution. This would require identical inherited and environmental risk combinations.

question: Monozygotic twins are discordant for a multifactorial trait. Under the assumptions of the twin-study model, which component most directly accounts for their phenotypic difference?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how twin studies and concordance values can be used to calculate heritability and what the value indicates

options.text: Different inherited allele combinations
options.rationale: Monozygotic twins are treated as mostly genetically identical. This would fit dizygotic twins or ordinary siblings.

options.text: Different degrees of genealogic relatedness
options.rationale: Both members have the same twin relationship. This would apply when comparing first- and third-degree relatives.

options.text: Different environmental influences
options.rationale: With genetic identity held approximately constant, discordance is attributed to environmental differences under the model's assumptions.

options.text: Different population prevalence values
options.rationale: Members of a twin pair do not acquire different phenotypes because of separate population prevalence values. This would matter when comparing distinct populations.

options.text: Different genome-wide association signals
options.rationale: Monozygotic twins are expected to share their inherited SNP pattern. This would fit genetically different case and control populations.

question: A highly associated SNP lies near a gene suspected of contributing to disease liability. Which statement most appropriately limits interpretation of this result?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how genome wide association studies work and how they can be used to identify genes that contribute to multifactorial conditions

options.text: The SNP necessarily determines the entire phenotype
options.rationale: A multifactorial phenotype reflects multiple genetic and environmental factors. This would require a deterministic single-gene condition.

options.text: The SNP proves environmental effects are absent
options.rationale: Genomic association does not exclude environmental influence. This would require total phenotypic variation to be genetic.

options.text: The SNP establishes complete familial concordance
options.rationale: An association does not mean all relatives share the phenotype. This would require complete expression among relatives carrying the variant.

options.text: The SNP may only mark a nearby contributor
options.rationale: The associated SNP may be located in or near a contributing gene and need not itself be the causal genetic factor.

options.text: The SNP defines the disease threshold value
options.rationale: A single SNP does not establish the numerical threshold for total liability. This would require complete measurement of all liability components.

question: Two exceptionally tall parents have a child who is tall compared with the population but shorter than either parent. Which principle best explains this pattern?
cited_learning_objective: Explain what is meant by regression to the mean

options.text: Sex-specific liability threshold
options.rationale: A liability threshold explains categorical disease expression rather than a child's position on a continuous trait distribution. This would fit a sex-biased present-or-absent condition.

options.text: Familial disease aggregation
options.rationale: Familial aggregation describes excess affected relatives rather than reduced extremeness in offspring. This would fit clustering of a disease within a family.

options.text: Twin-based heritability
options.rationale: Heritability measures genetic contribution to variance and does not specifically predict this parent-offspring pattern. This would require MZ and DZ concordance comparisons.

options.text: Genome-wide allelic association
options.rationale: Genome-wide association identifies SNP frequency differences between cases and controls. This would fit population-based localization of contributing genes.

options.text: Regression toward the mean
options.rationale: Offspring of parents at an extreme tend to remain on that side of the distribution while falling closer to the population mean.
